blocks.heading: How’s the New House? | kīf il‑bēt il‑jdīd? | كيف البيت الجديد؟
paragraphs: كِيف البَيْت الجْديد؟ (kīf il-bēt il-jdīd?)—“How’s the new house?”—is an easy, friendly question that can open the door to a real conversation in Southern Levantine Arabic. You can ask the same kind of question about a new apartment, car, school, neighborhood, or almost anything else in someone’s life.

This chapter begins with place. You will first learn prepositions and locative expressions that help you describe where people and things are: inside, outside, above, below, beside, behind, in front of, between, near, and far away.

Once you can describe where something is, you can begin talking about what a place contains. For example, you can say that there is a television in the living room, a book on the table, or a car in front of the house. These same patterns lead naturally into talking about possession.

From there, you will learn several ways to express possession: عِنْد (ʿind), مَع (maʿ), إلـ (il-), the إضافة (iḍāfa) structure, and common forms of تَبَع (tabaʿ). You will see how Southern Levantine Arabic distinguishes between things that a person has or owns and things that a house, room, car, or other object contains.

In English, possession and location may feel like separate topics. In Arabic, they often sit side by side. The patterns that help you say “in the house,” “next to the car,” or “behind the school” also help you talk about what is in a place, what someone has, and what belongs to whom.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to describe everyday spaces, locate people and objects, and talk more naturally about homes, belongings, and daily life.

blocks.heading: EVERYDAY EXPRESSION — “What God Has Willed.” | mā shāʾ Allāh | ما شاء الله
paragraphs: You will hear mā shāʾ Allāh all the time in Arabic. Literally, it means “what God has willed,” but in real conversation, people often use it when they see something nice, impressive, beautiful, successful, or worth admiring. Many speakers also say it to push away envy or the evil eye.

This expression is especially relevant in this chapter because you are learning how to talk about homes, rooms, things, and possession. If someone shows you their apartment, their house, their family, or something they are proud of, mā shāʾ Allāh is one of the most natural things to say.

It can feel like:
• “Wow, that’s beautiful.”
• “That’s really nice.”
• “God bless.”
• “That’s impressive.”

blocks.heading: 3.1 Prepositions & Locatives — ḥurūf il-jarr | حروف الجرّ
paragraphs: In English, prepositions are small but important words such as in, on, at, and behind. They show where one person or thing is in relation to another. Without them, we would not know whether someone is at home, in the kitchen, or behind the door. In other words, prepositions help us describe location and relationships in space.

Levantine Arabic works similarly, but it also uses location words and forms with attached pronouns that do not always match English word for word. Prepositions and location words generally come before the noun or phrase they relate to. So, to say that someone or something is at home, in the room, next to the bank, or behind the house, you simply use the appropriate preposition or location word with that place.
Remember from Chapter 2 that Arabic does not need a word for is. Instead of using a separate verb in a sentence like My dad is at home, Arabic places the location directly after the subject:
Notice that the sentence is complete even though there is no separate word for is. The subject is followed directly by its location.

You will also notice that some prepositions blend with the word that follows. For example, when بِـ (bi-, "in / at") comes before the definite article الـ (il-), the two merge in pronunciation and writing, producing forms like:
This is a normal part of how Levantine Arabic flows in everyday speech.

Prepositions can also attach directly to pronoun suffixes. This is how Arabic expresses phrases such as with me, on you, in it, or behind him. Instead of using a separate word for me, you, him, or her, Arabic attaches the pronoun directly to the preposition.

blocks.heading: Prepositions versus Locatives
paragraphs: Before moving on, it is helpful to understand one important distinction. Arabic has two main ways to talk about location: prepositions and locatives.
1. Simple Prepositions
Simple prepositions are short grammatical words that normally come directly before a noun, phrase, or attached pronoun.
Here are some of the most common simple prepositions:

عَلى / عَ | on; to — ʿala / ʿa
عَ الطّاوْلِة | on the table – ʿaṭ-ṭāwle
مَع صاحبي | with my friend – maʿ ṣāḥbī
مِن المَحَلّ | from the store – min il-maḥall
عَن الدَّرس | about the lesson – ʿan id-dars
عِنْد | at; at the place of – ʿind
عِنْد البَنْك | at the bank – ʿind il-bank

paragraphs: Notice that each preposition is immediately followed by a noun or phrase.
2. Locatives (Location Words)
Location words describe where someone or something is positioned: inside, outside, above, below, near, far, here, there, and so on.

blocks.heading: Usage
paragraphs: 1. Prepositions with Nouns
Prepositions must be followed by something. This can be either a noun or an attached pronoun.
Let’s look at the preposition “with”: مَع | with – maʿ
With a noun, the noun comes after the preposition, just as it does in English:
With a pronoun, the pattern works a little differently. In English, with me is written as two separate words. In Arabic, the pronoun attaches directly to the preposition:
The basic meaning stays the same, but the form changes depending on who or what follows the preposition.
Here are some common examples:

rows: بِالبَيْت | at home / in the house – bil-bēt
عَلى / عَ | on; to – ʿala / ʿa
عَ الطّاوْلِة | on the table – ʿaṭ-ṭāwle
مَع صاحْبي | with my friend – maʿ ṣāḥbī
مِن المَحَلّ | from the store – min il-maḥall

paragraphs: 2. Locatives With Nouns
Unlike prepositions, many location words can stand alone and complete the thought once a subject has been stated.
Let’s look at the location word “inside”: جُوّا | inside – juwwa

blocks.heading: Colloquial Features to Notice
paragraphs: As you learn Levantine Arabic, you’ll notice that some very common words change slightly in everyday speech. These aren’t different words—they’re simply the natural colloquial forms that native speakers use every day. Learning these patterns early will make spoken Arabic much easier to recognize and understand.

blocks.heading: عَلى (ʿala) with Pronoun Suffixes
paragraphs: When a pronoun suffix is attached, the shortened عَ (ʿa) is no longer used by itself. Instead, the preposition takes a slightly different form.
Look at these examples:
Notice that these forms use the عَلَيـ pattern rather than the shortened عَ that appears before nouns.
Compare:
Both come from عَلى, but the pronunciation changes depending on whether a noun or an attached pronoun follows.
For now, learn these common forms as complete expressions. You do not need to memorize another grammar chart.

blocks.heading: Best Way to Learn It
blocks.text:
As you work through this chapter, try to get away from translating every word one by one. Instead, learn each expression as a complete pattern.
For example, don’t think: ❌ قَريب مِن = “close” + “from”
Think: ✅ قَريب مِن = “close to”
Likewise, don’t think: ❌ بْعيد عَن = “far” + “about ”
Think:  ✅ بْعيد عَن = “far from”
This is true throughout Arabic. Many expressions are built differently than they are in English. If you focus on translating each individual word, you’ll often end up confused. Instead, train yourself to recognize the entire expression as a single idea.
As you hear and read these patterns repeatedly, they will begin to feel natural. Over time, you’ll stop translating in your head and start understanding Arabic the way native speakers do. That’s one of the biggest milestones in becoming fluent.

blocks.heading: جوّا (juwwa) & برّا (barra) Before Nouns
paragraphs: When جُوّا (juwwa) and بَرّا (barra) stand alone, they function as location words:
Before a following noun, speakers often use the connected forms juwwāt and barrāt, especially when specifying a particular place.
You will also hear:

Both patterns are common in everyday speech. Throughout this book, we’ll usually use جُوّات and بَرّات before nouns because they clearly express the meaning “inside of” or “outside of” a specific place.
The same thing happens when we want to attach a pronoun instead of naming the place or thing directly. The pronoun ending attaches to جُوّاتـ / بَرّاتـ:
For example, instead of saying “inside the hospital”, you can later refer back to the hospital simply as “inside it.”

blocks.heading: حَتّى (ḥatta) Before Another Word
paragraphs: The full word is حَتّى (ḥatta), meaning until, up to, or even, depending on the context.

In fast speech, you may hear ḥatta reduced before a following word, especially in common phrases. At this stage, recognize ta bukra and ta hallaʾ, but use the full form ḥatta in your own careful speech.
For example:

This shortening is especially common in fast, natural speech. Like عَ from عَلى, it is not a different word. It’s simply the everyday colloquial pronunciation of حَتّى when it is attached to the following word.

As you continue learning Arabic, you’ll notice many patterns like these. Rather than memorizing them as exceptions, think of them as the natural rhythm of spoken Levantine Arabic. The more you hear them, the more familiar—and intuitive—they will become.

blocks.heading: Note 1
blocks.text: لَحالُه (laḥālo) means “by himself” or “alone.” Strictly speaking, it is not a preposition or locative adverb, but an idiomatic adverbial expression. Its possessive ending changes according to the person: لَحالي (laḥāli), “by myself”; لَحالَك (laḥālak), “by yourself”; and لَحالها (laḥālha), “by herself.”

blocks.heading: Note 2
blocks.text: حَتّى (ḥatta) can mean “until” when referring to an endpoint, or “even” when adding emphasis.

blocks.heading: Note 3
blocks.text: بِـ / بـ (bi- / b-) attaches directly to the following word. Depending on the context, it can mean “in,” “at,” “with,” or “by.” فِي (fī) can also mean “in” or “at.” In everyday Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, فِي often emphasizes the idea of being inside a place, while بِـ is more commonly used for general location (e.g., بالبيت “at home,” بالجامعة “at the university”). Both are extremely common, and in many situations either one sounds natural.

blocks.heading: Note 4
blocks.text: عَ (ʿa) is the shortened colloquial form of عَلى (ʿala). Both commonly mean “on” or “to.”

blocks.heading: Note 5
blocks.text: بَلا (balā) and بِدون (bidūn) both mean “without.” بَلا (balā) is generally more colloquial, while بِدون (bidūn) is also common and widely understood.

blocks.heading: Note 1
blocks.text: بِالزاوية (biz-zāwye) literally means “in the corner.” To specify the corner of a room, speakers also commonly say بِزاوية الغُرْفِة (bizāwiyet il-ghurfe).

blocks.heading: Note 2
blocks.text: In Palestinian and Jordanian colloquial Arabic, بِـ (b-) is a bound preposition meaning “in, at, with, by,” while جُوّا (juwwa) means “inside” or “within.” With enclosed spaces—such as a house, restaurant, or box—both are often natural. However, while بِـ (b-) can sometimes mean “at” or refer to a place more generally, جُوّا (juwwa) makes it clear that something is physically inside.

blocks.heading: Note 3
blocks.text: دُغري (dughri) can mean “straight” (without turning), but it also commonly means “directly,” “right away,” or “honestly/directly,” depending on the context.

blocks.heading: Note 4
blocks.text: عَلى طول (ʿala ṭūl) literally means “the whole length.” In directions, it means “straight ahead” or “keep going straight.” In other contexts, it can also mean “all the time,” “constantly,” or “immediately,” depending on the situation.

blocks.heading: 3.2 Expressing Existence with fī
paragraphs: One of the most common and useful prepositions in Levantine Arabic is fī (في). You will hear it constantly because it does a lot of work in everyday speech.
At its most basic level, fī means “in” and functions as a preposition:

However, fī is not limited to this meaning. It also has a very important extended use that goes beyond a simple preposition. In everyday Arabic, fī is also used to express existence—what English expresses with “there is” or “there are.”
In this use, في (fī) introduces something that exists, is present, or is available.
Formula:  fī + noun (+ location)
So the sentence begins with the idea of “there is / there are,” and then introduces the thing being talked about. A location is often added, but not always required.

items.en: There is a book on the table.
There are people in the market.
There is coffee on the table.

paragraphs: One useful thing to notice is that fī does not change for singular or plural. English distinguishes between “there is” and “there are,” but Levantine Arabic uses fī for both.

blocks.heading: Negation: “There is no / There are no”
paragraphs: Negating this construction is different from negating a nominal sentence. In nominal sentences (X is Y), we usually use مِش (mish).

items.note: ↓ negated

paragraphs: With في (fī), however, we do not use مِش (mish). Instead, we add the negation ما (mā) before في (fī) to form ما في (mā fī). In other words:
ما (mā) + في (fī) = ما في (mā fī) — there is no / there are no

You’ll see ما (mā) again throughout this book. In both Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, ما (mā) is one of the most common ways to negate sentences. As you continue, you’ll learn how it is used with many other constructions, such as possession, desire, and past-tense expressions.

items.note: ↓ negated

items.en: There is no one at home.
items.note: ↓ negated. Footnote 1 on mā fī: It is often shortened even more in fast speech to مافي (māfi).

paragraphs: Remember: في (fī) stays the same for singular and plural.

items.en: There is a book on the table.
There are books on the table.

paragraphs: Likewise, ما في (mā fī) means both “there isn’t” and “there aren’t.”

blocks.heading: Past & Future Forms of في (fī) — “There Was / There Were” & “There Will Be”
paragraphs: So far, you have learned that في (fī) means there is / there are. It tells us that something exists, is present, or is available.

items.en: There is a book on the table.
There are people in the market.

paragraphs: Now let’s expand that idea.

Sometimes you need to talk about something that existed in the past. At other times, you need to say that something will exist in the future. Levantine Arabic makes this easy because both expressions are built around the في (fī) that you already know.
In this section, you will learn:
كان في (kān fī) — there was / there were
رَح يكون في (raḥ ykūn fī) — there will be

For now, think of each one as a complete expression. You do not need to analyze or conjugate كان (kān) or يكون (ykūn) yet. You will learn how they work as verbs later in Arabic After Verbs. Here, simply learn كان في and رَح يكون في as useful chunks of language.
Before we begin, let’s learn a few common time expressions that will help you talk about the past and future.

items.en: some time ago / a while ago

blocks.heading: Past: “There was / There were”
paragraphs: Formula: kān fī + noun (+ location / time) = There was/were ___ at/in/on ___.

items.en: There was a wallet on the table yesterday.

items.ar: كان في كُرسي جَنْب الكَنَبايِة قَبل.
items.translit: kān fī kursi janb il-kanabāye ʾabil
items.en: There was a chair next to the couch before.

items.ar: كان في قَهْوة بالمَطْبَخ مِن فَتْرة.
items.translit: kān fī ʾahwe bil-maṭbakh min fatra
items.en: There was coffee in the kitchen a little while ago.

items.ar: كان في حَدا عَالباب لأبوك اِمْبارح.
items.translit: kān fī ḥada ʿal-bāb la-abūk mbāriḥ
items.en: There was someone at the door for your dad yesterday.

blocks.heading: Negative Past: “There was no / There were no”
paragraphs: To say “there was no / there were no,” we put ما (mā) before كان في (kān fī)
Formula: mā + kān fī + noun (+ location / time) = There was no / There were no ___.

items.ar: ما كان في حَدا بالبيت قَبْل.
items.translit: mā kān fī ḥada bil-bēt ʾabil
items.en: There was no one at home before.

items.ar: ما كان في أَكِل بالمَطْبَخ مِن فَتْرة.
items.translit: mā kān fī akil bil-maṭbakh min fatra
items.en: There was no food in the kitchen a little while ago.

items.ar: ما كان في دَوا بالخِزانة امبارح.
items.translit: mā kān fī dawa bil-khizāne mbāriḥ
items.en: There was no medicine in the cabinet yesterday.

blocks.heading: Future “There will be”
paragraphs: يكون (ykūn) is related to كان (kān), and you’re going to see it a lot once we get into verbs. But we’re not there yet. For now, don’t worry about breaking it down or conjugating anything. Just learn رح يكون في (raḥ ykūn fī) as one useful chunk meaning “there will be.”
رح يكون في | raḥ ykūn fī — there will be
Formula: raḥ ykūn fī + noun (+ location / time) = There will be ___ at ___ time.

items.en: There will be a lesson tomorrow.

items.ar: رح يكون في ناس كتير بالحَفْلة
items.translit: raḥ ykūn fī nās ktīr bil-ḥafle
items.en: There will be a lot of people at the party.

items.ar: رح يكون في أَكِل عالطاوْلة بعدين
items.translit: raḥ ykūn fī akil ʿaṭ-ṭāwle baʿdēn
items.en: There will be food on the table later.

blocks.heading: Negative future “There will not be”
paragraphs: To say “there will not be / there will be no,” we put ما (mā) before رح يكون في (raḥ ykūn fī).
Formula: mā + raḥ ykūn fī = there will not be / there will be no

items.ar: ما رح يكون في وَقِت بُكْرا
items.translit: mā raḥ ykūn fī waʾt bukra
items.en: There will not be time tomorrow.

items.ar: ما رح يكون في حَدا بالبيت قَبْل العَشا
items.translit: mā raḥ ykūn fī ḥada bil-bēt ʾabl il-ʿasha
items.en: There will not be anyone at the house before dinner.

items.ar: ما رح يكون في أَكِل بالبيت بُكْرا
items.translit: mā raḥ ykūn fī akil bil-bēt bukra
items.en: There won’t be any food at home tomorrow.

items.ar: ما رح يكون في حَدا بالمَكْتَب بُكْرا
items.translit: mā raḥ ykūn fī ḥada bil-maktab bukra
items.en: There won’t be anyone at the office tomorrow.

blocks.heading: Main Idea
rows: there is no / there are no
there was no / there were no
there will not be / there will be no

blocks.text: For now, don’t worry about conjugating كان (kān) or يكون (ykūn). Just learn these expressions as useful chunks. You’ll get into how the verbs actually work later.

blocks.heading: Solo Drill — Describe the Apartment
paragraphs: You’ve learned the words you need to talk about where things are and what’s in a place. Now it’s time to put those pieces together on your own.
On the next page, you’ll see an apartment diagram. Look around the apartment and describe what you see. Use the location words you’ve learned to say where different things are.
For example, you might notice that something is in the kitchen, next to the couch, under the window, in front of the bed, or in the middle of the room.
Use في when you want to say that something is there:
في + thing + location

You don’t need to describe everything or have all the vocabulary memorized yet. Keep your vocabulary pages handy and use them when you need them. Choose different objects around the apartment and practice describing where they are. Say each sentence out loud and focus on putting the pieces together correctly. With repetition, it’ll start to come naturally.

blocks.heading: Then make it personal.
blocks.text:
Once you’re comfortable with the apartment on the next page, put the book down and look around your own room, apartment, or house.
Where’s your TV? What’s next to your bed? What’s in the kitchen? What’s behind the door? What’s in the middle of the room?
Do the exact same thing with your own space.
The goal isn’t to memorize the apartment in the book. The goal is to give you the tools to look at any space around you and start describing it in Arabic.
The more you do this with your real surroundings, the less this feels like a drill—and the more it starts feeling like Arabic you actually own.

blocks.title: “There Is” Drill
blocks.instructions:
Write the correct form of “there is / there are,” “there isn’t / there aren’t,” “there was / there were,” “there wasn’t / there weren’t,” “there will be,” or “there won’t be” in each blank, using the chunks you learned: في، ما في، كان في، ما كان في، رح يكون في، ما رح يكون في
Each sentence also has one missing noun from the vocabulary you learned. Write the correct noun in the blank.
Some sentences also include time expressions in English and Arabic. Pay attention to these expressions because they will help you determine whether the sentence refers to the present, past, or future.
Pay close attention to time and negation. Is the sentence talking about now, the past, or the future? Is something there, or not there? Once you know that, choose the right chunk, fill in the missing noun, and add the time expression when you need one.
This drill is long on purpose. By repeating the same chunks with different rooms, objects, and time expressions, you will build automaticity and make these patterns easier to use naturally when speaking.
Say everything out loud. Repetition is your friend.

blocks.heading: 3.3 Using ḥatta
paragraphs: The word ḥatta (حَتّى) is one of those small words that does a lot of work in Levantine Arabic. It appears constantly, and its meaning changes depending on the sentence.

For now, the three active meanings you need are:
• until
• even
• even if (in the fixed chunk ḥatta law حَتّى لَو)
Do not try to translate ḥatta with only one English word. Instead, look at what it is doing in the sentence.

blocks.heading: 1. ḥatta = until
paragraphs: Use ḥatta when you are talking about a limit in time. In this use, it means until.

items.en: I'm at home until the evening.
He is at the office until nighttime.

blocks.heading: 2. ḥatta = even
paragraphs: ḥatta can also mean “even.” Here, it adds emphasis by showing that someone or something you might not expect is included too.
Here’s how it looks in context:

items.en: Even the new jacket is expensive.

blocks.heading: 3. ḥatta law = even if
paragraphs: A very common phrase is:
حَتّى لَو | even if — ḥatta law
The word لَو (law) introduces a condition or possibility. You will learn how it works in greater detail when we begin studying verbs.
For now, think of حَتّى لَو as a complete expression meaning even if. It allows you to say that something remains true or that you still want something, regardless of a particular condition.
For example:

blocks.heading: Now look at some complete sentences:

items.en: I want the coffee even if it's expensive

items.ar: لِسّا بِدّي المَوْعِد حَتّى لَو بُكْرا
items.translit: lissa biddī il-mawʿid ḥatta law bukra
items.en: I still want the appointment even if it's tomorrow
The house is nice even if it's small

blocks.heading: What to Remember
blocks.text:
For now, associate حَتّى لَو with even if.
It introduces a condition that does not change the main idea of the sentence.

blocks.heading: 3.4 Human Possession
paragraphs: Possession in Arabic asks you to shift your thinking a bit, because it does not line up neatly with the English idea of “have” or the English apostrophe s (‘s). You will often be saying something that literally looks like “to me,” “with me,” or “for me,” rather than “I have.”

blocks.heading: Human Possession
paragraphs: We’re going to start this section with human possession, since that is probably what’s most relevant to your daily life. In English, we use the verb “have” for many different situations. We say:

- “I have a car.”
- “I have a sister.”
- “The room has a window.”
But these are not really the same kind of “having.”

You own the car.
You are related to the sister.
The window simply exists in the room.
Arabic treats these ideas more precisely.
Instead of relying on one all-purpose verb, Arabic uses different structures for different kinds of possession and association. It can be helpful to think of these as different logical “buckets.”
Each bucket answers a different question:

- Does something belong to a person?
- Is it physically with someone right now?
- Are you identifying the owner?
- Are you linking two nouns together?
- Are you simply saying that something exists somewhere?
Understanding these patterns will make your Arabic sound more natural and more precise.

In this section, we will begin with the “bucket” of human possession. This idea is a little more nuanced in Arabic than in English, because each class of possession uses a different preposition to signal it. As you work through the examples, focus on which question each structure is answering, rather than trying to force a single “have” into every sentence. Let’s dive in.

blocks.heading: Human Possession — Ownership & the Personal Sphere: عنده | ʿindo
paragraphs: The first structure is عِنْد (ʿind), which literally means “at.” You can think of it as placing something in your world — at you, within your sphere, under your ownership or responsibility. It does not mean the thing is physically in your hand right now. It means it belongs to your life.

عِنْد is used for:
• things you own
• family relationships
• things connected to your life in a broad sense
• abstract things in your possession, like plans, ideas, or appointments

In Southern Levantine Arabic, ʿind plus a possessive suffix is one of the main ways to express ‘have,’ especially for general possession, relationships, and things that are part of someone’s personal world.

items.note: The car belongs to me. It does not matter where it is parked right now — the point is ownership.
ʿind expresses family relationship here. The sister is part of her life and family circle.
This refers to family, not physical location. The children do not need to be standing next to us.

paragraphs: Now here is where it gets especially useful. ʿind is also the structure you use for things like questions, answers, plans, and ideas — the kinds of things students run into constantly in real conversation and in the classroom.

Note the difference: عِنْدي سُؤال means “I have a question” — indefinite, one of many possible questions. عِنْدي الجَواب means “I have the answer” — definite, a specific answer. The structure is the same; only the definiteness of the noun changes.

items.note: This is the negated form. ما before ʿind negates the possession entirely.

paragraphs: These examples come up constantly — in class, in conversation, and in daily life. Get comfortable with them early and they will serve you well throughout this book and beyond.

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text:
Use ʿind for:
• ownership
• family relationships
• general personal possession
• abstract possession: questions, answers, plans, time, appointments

blocks.heading: Human Possession — Immediate Physical Possession: معه | maʿo
paragraphs: You already know that عِنْد covers general ownership and possession — the things that belong to your world.
Now we move to a more immediate kind of having: what is physically on you, with you, or in your hand right now.
This is where مَع (maʿ ) comes in.
While عِنْد asks “Is this part of your life?”, مَع asks something much more immediate: “Is this on you right now?”
It is the difference between owning something and having it with you at this exact moment.

This distinction comes up constantly in real conversation. Think about how often you hear or say things like:
— Do you have your phone on you?
— I left my keys at home.
— Do you have any cash with you?
— I don’t have it on me right now.
A useful way to decide between عِنْد and مَع is to ask what kind of possession you want to emphasize.
عِنْد is commonly used when you are talking about something a person owns, has available, or has as part of their life.
مَع is commonly used when you want to emphasize that something is physically with a person at that moment.
Compare:

items.en: I have the house key with me

paragraphs: Both sentences are natural, but the focus is slightly different.
The first tells us that I have the key. The second specifically tells us that the key is with me right now.

blocks.heading: What to Remember
blocks.text:
Think of عِنْد as general possession or availability, and مَع as something being physically with someone.
This is a useful distinction, not an absolute rule. As you hear these expressions in real conversations, you will begin recognizing when speakers prefer one over the other.

items.note: The phone may still belong to me. But right now, I do not have it on me.

items.note: The book is in my bag or in my hand right now.

items.note: The papers are physically in his possession at this moment.

blocks.text:

• physical possession right now
• things you are carrying or holding
• immediate access
• things literally “with” someone
• asking or saying whether something is on someone at this moment
Quick Test:
Can you reach for it right now?
Yes → مَع
No, but it belongs to you → عِنْد
مَع is not mainly about ownership, it is about immediate presence. It tells us that something is with someone right now.

blocks.heading: Human Possession — Absolute Belonging
paragraphs: You now know two ways to talk about possession:
عِنْد tells us that something is part of someone’s life or personal world.
مَع tells us that something is physically with someone right now.
إلـ does something different.
It tells us who something belongs to. Instead of saying: “I have a book.” or: “I have the book with me.” إلـ lets you say: “The book is mine.”
The focus is not on having something. The focus is on identifying the owner.
Think of إلـ as answering the question: Whose is it?

Use this structure when:
ownership is being identified or clarified
you want to say that something is mine, yours, his, hers, ours, or theirs
you are distinguishing one person’s belongings from someone else’s
you are answering a question about who something belongs to
In everyday conversation, this comes up all the time. Someone may point to something and ask:

items.note: You can answer:

paragraphs: The basic pattern is: the thing + إلـ with a pronoun ending

items.note: We are not saying “I have a book.” We are identifying the owner of this specific book.
The focus is not that he has a car. The point is that this particular car belongs to him.
This identifies her as the owner of the bag.
This identifies us as the people the room belongs to.

paragraphs: Here is a useful contrast to keep these three structures clear in your mind:

items.note: General ownership, part of my life.

items.en: I have the car with me.
items.note: It is physically here with me right now.
This specific car belongs to me.

paragraphs: Same car. Three different statements. Three different structures.

blocks.heading: Negation
paragraphs: You already know how to use ما (mā) to make possession negative.
The same familiar pattern works with عِنْد, مَع, and إِلـ.
For example:

items.en: She doesn't have a key with her

paragraphs: But remember that إِلـ can also identify who something belongs to.
When you want to say that a particular thing does not belong to someone, you can use مِش (mish).
Notice the difference.
In the first sentence, we are saying that he doesn't have a notebook.
In the second, we are talking about a specific notebook and saying that it doesn't belong to him.

blocks.heading: What to Remember
blocks.text:
ما is a common way to negate possession with expressions like عِنْد and مَع.
When you are identifying ownership and want to say that a specific thing is not someone's, مِش إِلـ is another useful pattern.
The goal is to understand what kind of possession or ownership the sentence is expressing, rather than translating every English use of “have” the same way.

blocks.heading: 3.5 Non-human Possession
paragraphs: So far, the possession structures you have learned — عِنْد، مَع، and إِلـ — have focused mostly on people.
But Arabic also has specific ways to describe what a place or thing contains, includes, or is associated with. This is what we mean by non-human possession.
In English, we often use the verb “have” for all of this.

We say:
“The room has a window.”
“The apartment has a balcony.”
“The hotel has a pool.”

Arabic is more precise. It uses different structures depending on whether you are describing:
something physically inside a place or thing
or
something that belongs to it as a natural feature or part of it
Before we look at each structure, remember this rule:
The noun that “possesses” comes first. Then the possession construction refers back to it.

blocks.heading: Physical Containment — فيه | fīh
paragraphs: فِيه (fīh) and فِيها (fīha) both come from في (fī), meaning “in.” فِيه (fīh) refers back to a masculine noun. فِيها (fīha) refers back to a feminine noun.
Think of it as saying: “In it, there is…”
The focus is on what is contained inside the boundaries of a place or thing.

Important: فِيه / فِيها usually refer back to something already known in the sentence or conversation. “It” is not random. It points to a specific place or container that was mentioned or is clear from context. The attached pronoun must match the gender of that noun.
The basic formula is: [place] + فِيه / فِيها + [what is inside]

items.en: The house has a small kitchen.
items.note: Talking about a new house: The kitchen is physically inside the house.

items.en: The room has a big window.
items.note: Describing your classroom: The window is part of the room’s interior. غُرفة is feminine, so we use فِيها.

items.en: The neighborhood has a lot of shops.
items.note: Talking about your area: The shops are located within the neighborhood.
Telling someone about your daughter’s school: The classrooms are inside the school. مَدرسة is feminine, so we use فِيها.

blocks.heading: Negation
paragraphs: To negate this structure, add ما (mā) before فِيه / فِيها.

items.en: The house does not have a kitchen.
The room does not have a window.

blocks.heading: Inherent Attribution — إِلُه / إِلْها | ilo / ilha
paragraphs: إِلُه and إِلْها come from إِلـ (il-), which you already know from the human possession section (where it identifies the owner).

When used with non-human nouns, the meaning shifts slightly. Instead of pure ownership, it expresses that a feature or characteristic inherently belongs to something — it is part of what that thing is or comes with.

Think of it this way:
فِيه tells you what you will find inside.
إِلُه tells you what something comes with or is known for having.

blocks.heading: Important:
blocks.text: In natural Levantine speech (Jordanian, Palestinian, etc.), the two structures are sometimes interchangeable. But the nuance matters: فِيه leans toward physical contents inside a space, while إِلُه leans toward an inherent feature or attribute. إِلُه / إِلْها also refer back to a specific noun already mentioned or clear from context. The pronoun must match the gender of that noun (إِلُه for masculine, إِلْها for feminine).

items.en: The apartment has a sea view.
items.note: Talking about a new apartment you saw: (The sea view is a defining feature the apartment comes with.)

items.en: The house has a big backyard.
items.note: Describing a house in the suburbs: (The large yard is an inherent part of the house’s property.)

items.en: The hotel has a big entrance.
items.note: Recommending a hotel to friends: (The entrance is a feature the hotel comes with.)

blocks.heading: Main Idea
blocks.text:
Use فِيه / فِيها to describe what exists inside a place, and إِلُه / إِلْها to describe its features or characteristics.
These are useful distinctions, not strict rules. In everyday Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, the two structures can overlap.
For now, focus on recognizing how each one is commonly used.
